question: Is flaxseed omega-3 as good as fish oil for dogs?
answer: 🟡 Moderate evidence: No — and this is one of the most useful things to understand on a label. Flaxseed supplies ALA (alpha-linolenic acid). Fish, krill and algae supply EPA and DHA. Those are the forms that actually do the anti-inflammatory work, and a dog's body uses them directly. To get EPA and DHA out of flaxseed, a dog has to convert the ALA — and dogs convert it poorly, commonly cited at well under 10%, with conversion onward to DHA lower still. So a food built on flaxseed can show an excellent omega-6:3 ratio on paper while delivering a fraction of the usable omega-3 that number implies. Flaxseed isn't bad — it's fibre, lignans and some ALA. It just shouldn't be counted as equivalent to fish oil.
sources: Comparative canine fatty-acid metabolism; ALA-to-EPA/DHA conversion literature
source: Common Sense Dog — Omega Sources Pack

question: My dog food says it has a great omega-6 to omega-3 ratio. Can I trust that number?
answer: 🟡 Moderate evidence: Trust it as arithmetic, not as a promise. The ratio counts all omega-3 the same, whether it came from salmon oil or flaxseed — but your dog's body doesn't. Marine omega-3 (EPA/DHA) is usable on arrival; plant omega-3 (ALA, from flax, chia, canola, hemp) has to be converted at a rate well under 10%. The practical check takes five seconds: read the ingredient list and ask where the omega-3 is coming from, and how high up it sits. A food whose only omega-3 sources are flaxseed and chia has a real ratio and a weak delivery. A food with salmon oil, krill, sardines or algal oil is giving your dog the finished product.
sources: AAFCO labelling practice; canine fatty-acid conversion literature
source: Common Sense Dog — Omega Sources Pack

question: What are the best omega-3 sources for dogs?
answer: 🟢 Strong evidence for the marine forms: sardines (whole, in water, no salt added), salmon and salmon oil, herring, anchovy, mackerel, krill, green lipped mussel, and algal oil for a plant-based option that still supplies EPA/DHA directly. Algae is the exception among plant sources — it makes EPA and DHA itself, so no conversion is needed. ⚪ Whole-food first where you can: sardines give you EPA/DHA plus protein, calcium from the soft bones, and CoQ10, rather than an isolated oil. ⚠️ One caution: cod liver oil is a marine source but also concentrated in vitamins A and D, both of which accumulate. If a food already contains cod liver oil, adding more from a bottle can stack those. Plain fish oil and sardines don't carry that risk.
sources: Marine omega-3 EPA/DHA content; FDA vitamin A/D accumulation guidance

question: Why is the omega-6 to omega-3 ratio important for dogs?
answer: 🟡 Moderate evidence: Omega-6 and omega-3 compete for the same enzymes. Omega-6 (from chicken fat, sunflower, safflower, corn and soybean oils) feeds inflammatory pathways; omega-3, specifically EPA, feeds resolving ones. When the diet skews heavily to omega-6 the balance tips toward chronic low-grade inflammation — the background condition behind arthritis, skin flare-ups and lipomas. Holistic practice targets roughly 5:1 or lower; most kibble runs 15:1 to 30:1. ⚠️ Honest framing: the 5:1 target is practitioner guidance, not a controlled-trial endpoint. The underlying mechanism — EPA and DHA competing with arachidonic acid — is well established.
sources: Holistic veterinary practice consensus; established EPA/arachidonic acid competition mechanism
source: Common Sense Dog — Omega Sources Pack

question: Does my dog need fish oil if the food already has flaxseed?
answer: 🟡 Moderate evidence: Probably yes. Flaxseed contributes ALA, not EPA/DHA, and your dog converts very little of it. If flaxseed or chia are the only omega-3 sources on the label, the food is effectively asking your dog's metabolism to manufacture the active form — which it does badly. Adding sardines a few times a week, or a plain fish oil, supplies what's missing directly. If the food already contains salmon oil, krill or fish, the usable omega-3 is present and supplementing is optional rather than corrective. ⚠️ Educational only — dose matters, and high-fat additions need care in dogs with pancreatitis history. Ask your vet, ideally a holistic one, for amounts.
sources: Canine ALA conversion literature; clinical supplementation practice
source: Common Sense Dog — Omega Sources Pack

question: Is chia seed a good source of omega-3 for dogs?
answer: 🟡 Moderate evidence: Chia is in the same category as flaxseed — genuinely high in omega-3, but it is ALA, the plant form. The conversion problem is identical: dogs turn well under 10% of it into EPA, and less into DHA. Chia brings real value as soluble fibre and it counts toward a label's omega ratio, but it should not be read as equivalent to fish. If a food lists chia and flaxseed but no marine source, the usable omega-3 is thinner than the number suggests.
source: Common Sense Dog — Omega Sources Pack

question: Which ingredients are high in omega-6 in dog food?
answer: ⚪ Established formulation knowledge: The common ones are sunflower oil, safflower oil, corn oil, soybean oil, cottonseed oil and generic 'vegetable oil'. Poultry is the quieter contributor — chicken and duck fat are notably higher in omega-6 (linoleic acid) than beef, lamb or fish. Omega-6 isn't a villain; it's an essential fatty acid dogs require for skin, coat and cell function. The issue is proportion. A poultry-based food using sunflower or corn oil as its fat source, with only flaxseed for omega-3, is where ratios climb into the 15:1 to 30:1 range.
sources: Fatty-acid composition of common pet food fats; pet food formulation practice
source: Common Sense Dog — Omega Sources Pack

question: Is algae oil a good omega-3 source for dogs?
answer: 🟡 Moderate evidence: Yes — and it's the one plant-derived exception worth knowing. Algae produce EPA and DHA directly, which is where fish get theirs from in the first place, so algal oil delivers the usable forms without the conversion problem that limits flaxseed and chia. It's a genuine option for dogs with fish sensitivities, and it avoids the heavy-metal and sustainability questions around some fish oils. Typically more expensive per unit of EPA/DHA than fish oil.
sources: Algal EPA/DHA composition; marine food chain origin of EPA/DHA

question: Is there a clinical trial proving omega-3 helps dogs with arthritis?
answer: 🟢 Strong evidence: Yes — Roush et al. (2010, Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association 236(1):59–66, PMID 20043800). A randomised, double-blinded, controlled trial run across 18 private veterinary clinics with 127 client-owned dogs with osteoarthritis. Dogs were fed for six months on either a typical commercial food or a test food with a 31-fold increase in total omega-3 and a 34-fold decrease in the omega-6:omega-3 ratio. Blood work confirmed the diet did what it claimed: significantly higher serum omega-3 and significantly lower arachidonic acid at 6, 12 and 24 weeks. Owners reported significantly improved ability to rise from rest and to play by 6 weeks, and improved walking at 12 and 24 weeks. This is one of the better-designed nutrition trials in dogs — randomised, blinded, controlled, multicentre, with both a biochemical and a clinical endpoint.
sources: Roush JK, Dodd CE, Fritsch DA, Allen TA, Jewell DE, Schoenherr WD, Richardson DC, Leventhal PS, Hahn KA. 2010. J Am Vet Med Assoc 236(1):59-66. PMID 20043800
source: Common Sense Dog — Omega Sources Pack

question: Is a lower omega-6 to omega-3 ratio than 5:1 even better for dogs?
answer: 🟡 Moderate evidence, and the direction of travel says yes. The 5:1 figure is a practical target, not a ceiling on benefit. Reviews of the canine literature put the anti-inflammatory range from roughly 5.5:1 at the upper end down to about 1:3.75 — that lower figure being an inverted ratio, with nearly four times more omega-3 than omega-6. The strongest single trial (Roush et al., 2010) used a food with a 34-fold reduction in the ratio and produced measurable clinical improvement in arthritic dogs over six months. ⚠️ Two honest caveats. Omega-6 is an essential fatty acid dogs genuinely require for skin and coat, so driving it toward zero isn't the goal. And what actually matters is the absolute amount of EPA and DHA delivered — a ratio achieved by cutting omega-6 rather than adding marine omega-3 looks identical on paper and does much less.
sources: Reviews of canine dietary n-6:n-3 ratio and inflammatory endpoints
source: Common Sense Dog — Omega Sources Pack

question: What foods are high in omega-6 for dogs, and does my dog get enough?
answer: 🟢 Strong evidence, and the answer is almost certainly yes. Omega-6 (linoleic acid) is an essential fatty acid — dogs cannot synthesise it — and AAFCO sets a minimum of 1.1% dry matter for adult maintenance, 1.3% for growth. Richest sources, roughly in order: sunflower, safflower, corn, soybean and grapeseed oils (near-pure omega-6, and what pushes commercial ratios to 20:1 or worse); then poultry — chicken fat, chicken, duck, turkey — which is the highest among common meats; then pork, egg yolk, and nuts and seeds. Organ meats carry a moderate amount alongside dense vitamins and minerals. Beef, lamb and venison sit meaningfully lower, which is why a beef formula often shows a better ratio than a chicken one. ⚪ In practice, omega-6 deficiency is close to unheard of on any meat-based diet. Deficiency would show as poor coat, skin problems, slow wound healing and weakened immunity. The reason the omega-6:3 ratio matters is that omega-6 is abundant and omega-3 is scarce — the lever worth pulling is adding marine omega-3, not cutting omega-6.
sources: AAFCO Dog Food Nutrient Profiles — linoleic acid minimum 1.1% DM adult maintenance, 1.3% growth

question: Do dogs need arachidonic acid like cats do?
answer: 🟢 Strong evidence: No — this is one of the real metabolic differences between the species. Arachidonic acid (AA) is an omega-6 fatty acid that cats must get preformed from the diet, because they lack sufficient delta-6 desaturase to make it from linoleic acid. Dogs have that enzyme and convert linoleic acid to arachidonic acid perfectly well, so AA is not a dietary essential for them. Practical consequence: a plant-oil-based fat source can meet a dog's omega-6 needs but not a cat's, which is one reason cat food cannot simply be dog food with a different label — and why feeding cat food to a dog, or vice versa, isn't a like-for-like swap.
sources: Comparative essential fatty acid requirements, dogs vs cats (delta-6 desaturase activity)
source: Common Sense Dog — Omega Sources Pack
